articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Shadow Banking Network and Exchange Houses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 23, 2026. These actions target more than two dozen exchange houses, front companies, and individuals identified as part of Iran's global shadow banking networks.

These designations fall under Operation Economic Outcast, an initiative aimed at severing Iran's remaining financial lifelines. The targeted entities are alleged to facilitate Iran's access to foreign currency and international trade, underpinning much of its remaining foreign commerce.
The sanctions were imposed pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, E.O. 13224, as amended, and E.O. 13871, which target specific sectors of the Iranian economy and persons operating within them.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Iranian Oil Traders and Issues Cuba FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran designations on November 20, 2026, targeting individuals involved in facilitating Iranian oil sales and supporting previously designated entities.

These actions are part of Operation Economic Outcast, which aims to disrupt Iran's ability to sell oil abroad and recoup revenue. The Treasury Department stated that the action was imposed under two executive orders: one targeting Iran's petroleum, petrochemical, and aviation sectors, and the other a counterterrorism authority.
Concurrently, OFAC issued new Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) related to Cuba sanctions, providing guidance on existing restrictions.

articles.headline: OFAC Targets Narcotics and Cyber Networks, Amends Russia-Related GL
body: On November 19, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting counter narcotics and cyber-related activities.

The designations include individuals and entities tied to international narcotics trafficking, specifically targeting the Italian 'Ndrangheta and the Comanchero Outlaw Motorcycle Gang under Executive Order 14059.

Additionally, OFAC issued an Illicit Drugs General License and an amended Russia-related General License, along with updated Frequently Asked Questions, to provide clarity and authorize certain transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) implemented new counter terrorism designations on November 18, 2026. These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt financial support for terrorist organizations globally.
The specific individuals or entities targeted in these designations were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but fall under OFAC's broader counter-terrorism authorities.
These designations aim to prevent the flow of funds and resources to groups and individuals involved in terrorist activities, thereby safeguarding the U.S. financial system from illicit finance.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: On November 13, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under both its counter narcotics and counter terrorism authorities. This dual action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to combating various forms of illicit activity.
These designations aim to disrupt the financial networks of individuals and entities involved in drug trafficking and those providing material support to terrorist organizations.

The specific details of the designated parties were not immediately released, but these actions are consistent with OFAC's strategy of using financial sanctions to protect national security and foreign policy interests.

Such updates are routine and ensure the accuracy and effectiveness of sanctions programs by providing clearer guidance to financial institutions and other regulated entities.
The specific nature of the update was not detailed in the initial announcement but is part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to maintain the integrity of its sanctions lists.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: On November 6, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations. These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing pressure campaign against the Iranian regime.
The designations aim to target individuals and entities supporting Iran's destabilizing activities and its various illicit programs.
Further details on the specific targets and the rationale behind these designations are typically provided in accompanying press releases or statements from the Treasury Department.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Cuban Entities, Targets Chinese Companies for First Time
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations designations, alongside Cuba designations and the publication of a Cuba-related determination on November 5, 2026.

For the first time, these new sanctions against Cuba include Chinese companies among their targets, specifically China National Electronics Import & Export Corporation (CEIEC) and Beijing H&C Technologies. These companies were accused of supplying equipment to Cuba's military through a Cuban procurement firm.

The sanctions also target several Cuban companies involved in the transport of crude oil and other petroleum products, as well as CUBAELECTRONICA and TECNOSIME. This action is seen as an escalation of the Trump administration's economic pressure campaign against Cuba.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / World Socialist Web Site

Alongside these actions, OFAC published an Iran-related OFAC Alert and issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and Frequently Asked Question.

The amended Venezuela-related General License and FAQ provide updated guidance for certain transactions involving Venezuela, reflecting ongoing policy adjustments in response to the country's political and economic situation.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are typically issued to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs, often to facilitate humanitarian aid, personal communications, or other specific activities.
The specific changes introduced by this amended General License would require a review of the updated text on the Treasury website for full details.

articles.headline: EU Proposes 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Banks, Crypto, and Energy
body: On November 23, 2026, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen presented the proposed 22nd package of EU sanctions against Russia. The comprehensive package aims to expand restrictions on Russian banks, crypto and payment networks, energy services, and maritime transport.

Key proposals include extending the transaction ban to approximately 60 Russian banks and disconnecting them from SWIFT, as well as targeting crypto and payment networks in Russia and third countries facilitating circumvention. The Commission also announced the launch of a Crypto Sanctions Task Force to support these efforts.

The package further proposes broadening the energy services ban to cover services supporting the construction, operation, or repair of Russian energy infrastructure, including refineries, and extending it to electricity services for the first time. Restrictions on positions in governing bodies of companies in Russia, a visa ban for former Russian combatants, and limitations on Russian teams and athletes in EU sporting events are also included.

articles.headline: EU Restricts Trade with 15 Russian Entities Linked to Military-Industrial Complex
body: On November 25, 2026, the Council of the European Union decided to add 15 Russian entities to the list of those subject to tighter export restrictions on dual-use goods and advanced technologies.

These entities are identified as part of Russia's military and industrial complex, with links to or providing support for Russia's defense and security sector. This action is intended to further increase pressure on Russia to end its war of aggression in Ukraine.

The Council also decided to remove one entity from the list, citing that the entity had ceased the behavior that led to its listing and provided credible assurances against trading sensitive goods with Russia.

articles.headline: WHO Calls for Lifting of U.S. Oil Blockade on Cuba Amid Humanitarian Crisis
body: World Health Organization (WHO) chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called for the immediate lifting of the U.S. fuel blockade on Cuba, warning that the measure is endangering the lives of children and causing direct harm to the Cuban people.

The UN has repeatedly warned of a growing humanitarian crisis on the island, stating that the U.S. fuel blockade violates international law and the human rights of all Cubans. Cuba has experienced prolonged power outages, water shortages, and critical medicine scarcity due to the embargo.

The Cuban government reports daily power outages lasting 20 hours or more, critical shortages of medicines and surgical supplies, and a decline in health indicators, including infant mortality rates. Washington maintains that the energy blockade aims to push for political change and that exports of food and medicine are legally exempt.

articles.headline: BIS Implements New Export Controls on Advanced Semiconductors and Remote Access to AI Capabilities
body: On November 16, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued an interim final rule (IFR) titled 'Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors,' which became effective upon publication in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. This rule introduces significant new export controls on advanced computing items, including advanced semiconductors, and targets certain foreign data center activities involving remote access to computing power.

The IFR establishes new end-use controls requiring a license for the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of advanced computing items if there is knowledge that they will be used in a data center providing significant computing power (greater than 12,000,000 aggregate total processing performance) to an entity headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent is headquartered in, Macau or a Country Group D:5 destination (including China). It also imposes a new destination-based license requirement for exports of advanced computing items to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil, citing a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.

Additionally, the rule formally rescinds the Biden-era 'AI Diffusion Rule,' which BIS had previously announced it would not enforce. Companies operating along global semiconductor and artificial intelligence supply chains, particularly data center operators and exporters of advanced computing components, are advised to review and update their export compliance procedures.
articles.source: U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security / Federal Register

articles.headline: BIS Adds Seven Entities in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand to Entity List
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amended the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by adding seven entities to the Entity List under the destinations of Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This rule is effective November 23, 2026.

These entities have been determined by the U.S. Government to be acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States due to a significant risk of involvement in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users.

For each listed entity, a license is now required for all items subject to the EAR, and license applications will be reviewed under a presumption of denial. A savings clause allows certain shipments already en route on November 23, 2026, to proceed under previous eligibility if completed by December 23, 2026.
articles.source: Federal Register / U.S. Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security

articles.headline: Addressing Remote Access to Advanced Semiconductors
body: In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. The regulatory changes in this rule formalize the rescission of the AI Diffusion Rule, which the Department of Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced in May 2025.

articles.headline: Extension of the Suspension of Expansion of End-User Controls for Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is extending the suspension of the interim final rule (IFR), "Expansion of End-User Controls to Cover Affiliates of Certain Listed Entities." The suspension was set to end November 9, 2026. This final rule extends the suspension through January 10, 2027.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
